title: You Are Not Your Personality Test
author: By Title Only
summary: By Title Only argues that personality tests grounded in the Big Five model — Myers-Briggs, DiSC, CliftonStrengths and others — are psychologically credible measurement tools that most people badly misuse, treating a snapshot of current behavioral habits as a fixed diagnosis of permanent identity. Using the image of an unflattering photograph taken mid-stride, the author shows how people take their results and then use them to explain and justify their behavior instead of changing it. Research shows traits can shift significantly in as little as fifteen weeks, so the same test at different career stages would produce meaningfully different results. The reframe for leaders is that test results are questions, not statements: a trait score asks whether a pattern that once served you is still serving you now, and habits that no longer help can be changed.
points: Big Five tests measure five behavioral tendencies on spectra (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism); they capture current pattern tendencies, not a fixed identity.
The core error is using a credible-looking result as a diagnosis and then explaining behavior with it ('I can't help it, I'm an introvert') rather than changing the behavior.
Personality traits change over time — research shows they can shift significantly in as little as 15 weeks — so a test reveals current habits, not a permanent self.
The reframe: your test results are not statements but questions, asking whether a given pattern is still benefitting you.
A low Openness score or high Conscientiousness score that once made you a reliable individual contributor can be exactly what holds you back as a leader — and can be deliberately changed.
quotes: So you use the results to explain your behavior, instead of changing your behavior.

It’s like taking a snapshot of your current behavioral patterns, and then believing that picture represents the same exact person you were five years ago and the same one you’ll be five years from now.
Research consistently shows that personality traits change over time. In fact, they can change significantly in as little as 15 weeks.
That means your personality test doesn’t reveal your true identity - it only reveals your current habits.
Your test results aren’t statements, they’re questions. They’re not telling you who you are as much as asking you if your patterns are still benefitting you.

When you stop looking at your personality test as a crystal ball and start understanding it’s just a photograph in time, you can start using the information in your favor to help guide the changes you need, and be the person you want.
Your personality test didn’t ever limit you. You’re the one that gave it that power.
